vignette:
Marco often says his body was his first language, the one he knew before he could properly speak. For fifty years, it was a language of precision and passion. As a young man in Buenos Aires, it spoke the sharp, staccato dialect of tango. In New York, it learned the fluid grammar of modern dance. Now, at sixty-two, it was the language he used to teach, his hands shaping the air, his posture demonstrating a line for his students, a subtle shift of weight conveying more than words ever could. He and his wife, Elena, had built their life around this shared language of movement, running a small but respected dance studio.

That language was silenced on a Tuesday afternoon in May. He was heading to the studio, humming along to a Piazzolla track on the radio, when a delivery truck ran a red light. Marco remembers three distinct things from the collision: the sun glinting off the truck’s chrome grill an instant before impact, a horn blaring a sound that was far too close, and then the brutal percussion of metal on metal. The world became a kaleidoscope of shattering glass and a violent, spinning chaos. When it stopped, there was a terrifying silence, broken only by the tick-tick-ticking of his turn signal and a strange, high-pitched ringing in his ears. He looked down and saw his left leg bent at an angle that defied anatomy. That’s when the pain began.

It has been eight months since the accident. The leg, after two surgeries and countless hours of physical therapy, has healed into a new, unfamiliar shape. It is functional, the doctors say, but it is no longer an instrument of art. It aches with the weather and protests when he stands for too long. But the injury to the limb is nothing compared to the injury to his mind.

Marco has not driven since that day. The driver's seat of their car feels like a coffin. Elena drives him everywhere now, taking meandering back roads to avoid the intersection where it happened. Even as a passenger, he is a terrible co-pilot, his foot slamming an imaginary brake pedal, his hands gripping the dashboard until his knuckles are white. The city, once a stage, is now a minefield of triggers. The screech of a bus’s air brakes sends a jolt of ice through his veins. The smell of gasoline at a filling station once made him feel dizzy and nauseous, convinced he was back in the mangled car, smelling a fuel leak. He had to get out and gasp for air on the concrete while Elena paid.

Sleep offers little escape. He lies awake for hours, his mind replaying the crash, editing it, trying to find a different outcome. What if he had left five minutes later? What if he’d taken a different street? When he does sleep, the dreams come—not of the crash itself, but of being trapped, of spinning endlessly in the dark. He often wakes up with his heart hammering against his ribs, the sheets damp with sweat.

The joy has been leached from his life. The tango music he once loved now sits silent on the shelf. He stopped going to the studio. He told Elena the students were better off with a teacher who could fully participate, but the truth is he can’t bear to be in that room. He feels like a ghost watching a life that is no longer his. He is irritable and distant, snapping at Elena over small things, then retreating into a stony silence, consumed by a guilt he can’t articulate. He spends most of his days in his armchair, staring out the window, a spectator in the life he once choreographed with such grace. His body, his oldest and most trusted friend, now feels like a stranger, a constant, aching reminder of the moment everything changed.
